name: Almost All Jobs Are R&D
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Research, Not Yet Engineering
lesson.summary: Nearly every job in quantum computing today is a research and development role rather than a mature production engineering role, and that distinction, more than any specific job title, is the single most important thing to understand before planning a career in the field.
lesson.body:
Engineers and researchers often get lumped together in casual conversation, but the two kinds of work differ in ways that matter enormously for career stability. Mature engineering work happens on top of a stable foundation: known techniques, established best practices, and a product with a defined purpose that mostly needs building, maintaining, and incrementally improving. Research and development work happens where that foundation does not exist yet: the fundamental questions are still open, techniques are still being invented, and a meaningful fraction of projects are expected to fail or dead end entirely, because that is simply how exploratory research works. As the previous chapter established, the quantum computing job market is small and concentrated in exactly this second category.

This shows up concretely in what the actual work looks like. A software engineer at a mature company spends most of their time writing, testing, and shipping code within well understood frameworks, where success is measured by shipped features and reliability. A quantum computing researcher, even one with an "engineer" job title, more often spends their time running experiments whose outcomes are genuinely uncertain, iterating on hardware or algorithms that may not work at all, and writing up results whether or not they represent progress. Both kinds of work require real skill and intelligence, but they carry very different risk profiles: mature engineering work is judged mostly by execution, while research work is judged partly by execution and partly by factors outside any individual's control, like whether the underlying physical approach turns out to be viable at all.

The career implication is that job security in an R&D heavy field tracks the funding cycle far more tightly than it tracks individual performance. A talented, hardworking researcher on a well regarded team can still lose their position if a funding agency shifts priorities, if a company's internal research budget gets cut during a difficult quarter, or if a particular experimental approach, such as a specific qubit modality, falls out of favor relative to a competing approach. This is simply a structural feature of research funded work, not a comment on any individual's competence, but it means the usual career advice of "just be good at your job and you will be fine" applies less cleanly here than it does in mature engineering fields.

Understanding this distinction is not a reason to avoid quantum computing entirely. Research careers can be deeply rewarding, and someone drawn to open, unsolved problems may actively prefer this kind of work over the more repetitive rhythms of mature product engineering. But going in with an accurate picture, that this is overwhelmingly a research field right now rather than an engineering field with research on the side, changes how a student should plan financially, how much they should diversify their skills, and how closely they should track the funding landscape around their specific specialty. That preparation is the subject of the ethics chapter that follows.
